name: AC-262536
lead: AC-262,536 (also called Accadrine) is an experimental nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed by Acadia Pharmaceuticals. A 2008 pharmacological characterisation described it as a potent, selective androgen receptor ligand with partial agonist activity, and in a 2-week study in castrated male rats it improved anabolic parameters.[1][2]

People who use it are seeking more lean muscle, and in some cases a fuller frame, because androgen-receptor activation is the pathway through which testosterone builds muscle, and SARMs are designed to favour muscle and bone over prostate and other reproductive tissue.[1][5] In the 2008 rat work, AC-262,536 stimulated growth of the levator ani muscle, a muscle used as a measure of anabolic effect, with weak effects on prostate and seminal vesicle weight.[1] Wikipedia reports that its maximal effect on levator ani weight was about 66% of testosterone's, against about 27% for prostate weight.[2]

It has not been approved for any use and no human trial was identified. It was encountered as a designer drug sold online by at least 2020, and anti-doping laboratories have since built detection methods for it.[2][3][4][8] On looksmax.org it is discussed as a milder oral alternative to anabolic steroids and as part of frame-building stacks.[6][7]

paras: People who take SARMs outside research do so for lean mass, a harder-looking physique and, in some forum discussions, frame and bone growth. On looksmax.org AC-262 is described as an oral option for people who do not want injectables, and as a milder alternative to steroids.[6][7] One thread asks about oral options aimed at more bone, shoulder width and possibly height, listing AC-262 alongside MK-677 among oral candidates.[6] The compound is sold online as a supplement-style product, and sports-testing researchers describe SARMs as a doping-control concern because of their growth- and bone-promoting effects.[3][8]

No approved medical use exists. The 2008 paper framed non-steroidal SARMs as a possible advance over testosterone therapy given the limitations of current treatments, which is the setting for which Acadia studied it.[1]

AC-262,536 binds the androgen receptor with a reported Ki of about 5 nM, against 29 nM for testosterone and 10 nM for DHT, and showed no significant affinity for other receptors tested.[1][2] Wikipedia describes it as a tissue-selective partial agonist of the androgen receptor.[2] In the 2008 paper, it suppressed elevated luteinising hormone in castrated rats, a sign of activity at the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.[1]

How SARMs achieve tissue selectivity is still debated. Wikipedia lists hypotheses including lack of activation by 5-alpha reductase, tissue-specific coregulator expression, non-genomic signalling and tissue-selective uptake, and says radiolabelled studies did not support the uptake hypothesis.[5] David Handelsman has called the term SARM a misleading marketing term rather than an accurate pharmacological description.[5]

The molecule is 4-[(1R,3S,5S)-3-hydroxy-8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octan-8-yl]naphthalene-1-carbonitrile, with formula C18H18N2O. It exists as endo and exo isomers, and the endo form is the active one. It is an aniline-type SARM related to ACP-105 and vosilasarm (RAD140).[2] A urine-screening paper classes it as a tropanol derivative among nine chemical classes of SARMs.[4]

The SARM concept grew out of interest in tissue-selective drugs after selective estrogen receptor modulators such as tamoxifen proved useful. Wikipedia reports that the first nonsteroidal SARMs were developed in 1998 by a University of Tennessee group and by Ligand Pharmaceuticals, and that the term was introduced in 1999.[5] Acadia Pharmaceuticals developed AC-262,536 as part of this wave, and in 2008 Piu and colleagues published its characterisation using a cell-based assay and a 2-week study in castrated male rats.[1][2] No clinical development was reported, and Wikipedia classes it as an abandoned drug.[2]

By 2020 it was being found as a novel designer drug. Laboratories have since built methods to detect it in horse blood, equine urine, plasma and hair, and in human urine.[3][4][8] WADA banned SARMs in 2008, according to Wikipedia.[5]

sections.h: The SARM class in human research
paras: Other SARMs have been tested in people. A 12-week, double-blind phase II trial of enobosarm (GTx-024) in 120 healthy adults over 60 reported dose-dependent increases in DXA-measured lean body mass, improved physical function, and adverse event rates similar to placebo.[9] Wikipedia notes that as of 2023 no SARM had FDA or EMA approval and that many candidates were discontinued.[5] Findings from other compounds do not carry over automatically to AC-262,536, which has no human data.

No studies found in humans. Published research on AC-262,536 is preclinical: the 2008 rat study reported improved anabolic parameters over two weeks.[1] The remaining literature is analytical work on equine metabolism, in which nine phase I metabolites were identified in vitro and the parent drug and several metabolites were detected in urine and plasma after oral administration to two Thoroughbred horses, plus detection methods for doping control.[3][4][8]

No human safety data were identified for AC-262,536. For the SARM class, Wikipedia reports that trial adverse events were generally mild and infrequent, with possible raised liver enzymes, lower HDL cholesterol and some suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.[5]

A 2023 systematic review of safety in healthy adults included 33 studies (15 case reports or series and 18 trials, 2,136 patients, 1,447 exposed to SARMs). It found 15 liver injury cases, one Achilles tendon rupture and one rhabdomyolysis case among the case reports, mean ALT elevation in 7.1% of trial participants, and two cases of rhabdomyolysis in a GSK2881078 trial.[10] A 2024 review of suspected adverse events found 20 reports since 2020, most describing drug-induced liver injury, with limited data on dose and product purity.[11] A case report described a 24-year-old man who developed severe jaundice after taking enobosarm for muscle building and needed albumin dialysis, with bilirubin taking about six months to normalise.[12]

A 2025 systematic review of athlete abuse reported that an estimated 1 to 3% of athletes use SARMs, that most bought the products online where they were often contaminated, and that users typically took doses far above those studied clinically.[13] The Endocrine Society's scientific statement on performance-enhancing drugs notes that users often combine several compounds, which complicates attributing harms.[14]

AC-262,536 is not approved by the US FDA for any medical use.[2] Wikipedia cites an FDA 2017 warning against SARMs in bodybuilding products, and the FDA has stated that SARMs are unapproved and cannot legally be marketed as supplements or drugs.[2][5] Researchers note that SARMs are nonetheless sold online as supplement-style products.[3] SARMs are on the WADA prohibited list, and anti-doping laboratories screen for them.[5][8]

lore.intro: AC-262536 is discussed on looksmax.org in threads about building muscle and frame, often as an oral option for people who do not want injectables. [6][7]

claims.claim: It can add several kilograms of lean mass with minimal side effects
claims.believers: A forum poster states that it can give roughly 5 kg of lean mass over several weeks, with low suppression and mild effects. [7]
claims.experts: No published human study has measured its effect on muscle or hormones. The only efficacy data come from castrated rats. [1]

claims.claim: It has little suppressive effect on natural hormones
claims.believers: Users argue that suppression is low to none and recovers without further measures. [7]
claims.experts: The 2008 rat study reported suppression of luteinising hormone in castrated animals, and reviews of the SARM class describe suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in some trials. [1][5]

claims.claim: Oral SARMs can support bone and frame growth
claims.believers: One poster looking to increase bone mass, shoulder width and possibly height asked about oral options. [6]
claims.experts: No human study has examined AC-262536 for bone or height. [1]

claims.claim: It is a safer route than anabolic steroids
claims.believers: Posters describe it as a milder choice for people wary of steroid side effects. [7]
claims.experts: No human safety data exist for it, and the US FDA states that SARMs are unapproved and cannot legally be marketed as supplements or drugs; reviews describe liver enzyme elevation and lowered HDL cholesterol in some SARM trials. [5]

claims.claim: Oral SARMs are the low-profile way to add muscle without injections
claims.believers: One poster said they did not want results to 'scream compound' and described AC-262 as decent and the safest option available to them.[7]
claims.experts: Anti-doping laboratories have developed urine, blood and hair methods that detect AC-262536, and reviews report liver injury and contamination in the SARM marketplace.[3][4][10][13]

card.summary: An Acadia-developed experimental SARM with rat data and no human trials, sold online as a research chemical.
card.note: Preclinical only; unapproved; banned in sport.

quick.overview:
AC-262536 is an experimental SARM from Acadia Pharmaceuticals. Rat studies showed muscle-building effects with smaller prostate effects than testosterone.

It has never been tested in a published human trial.
quick.mechanism: It is a partial agonist of the androgen receptor with reported tissue selectivity in rats.
quick.risks: Human safety is unknown. As an unapproved SARM it is banned in sport, and the class is linked in reports to liver injury and hormone suppression.

chain: Binds the androgen receptor as a partial agonist
Stimulates muscle-type tissue growth in rats with weaker prostate effect
Claimed: more lean mass for a fuller physique
angle.text: People who use it are seeking added lean muscle mass without the full androgenic effect of testosterone. The only published efficacy data are from castrated rats; no human trial of muscle gain exists.
